utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Before I proceed with my cross-examination, I should like to I apologise to you for the manner in which I cross-examined you on Friday [sic]. Please receive my apologies. I hope I did not hurt your feelings. If I did, please do receive the apologies. If you will remember, I mentioned only your first name, and you thought that that could perhaps reveal your identity, but please understand that was not my intention, by no means. I merely wanted to find out, as we have two documents, two different names, and they are completely different, I merely wanted to establish the difference. So please receive my apologies, and my apologies go both to you and the Chamber. Please also understand that I am the counsel for the Defence. It is my job to check everything that was said during the direct examination. I will do my best today to do that, that is, to conduct my cross-examination in as composed, in as calm a manner as possible, and I should like to invite you to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry. I'm not getting the interpretation. The headset is not working. So could somebody please help me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please have it checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, do you own up to this statement? Do you accept it as your own; and is it truthful as a whole; and the signature on the statement, is it your signature or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember signing it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the witness mentions the spelling of his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then let us -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we go back to the private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. There are five different signatures. I've been given again the same kind of paper that I was given before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go back to the private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the same paper here as before, gentlemen. I am really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You see it on page 3, above the mention of the 26th of May, 1999. So below that, rather. The last paragraph. One, two, three -- third sentence: "They took me to the old building of the KP Dom, the penal and correctional institution."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that was the building. I'm not quite sure whether it was that building, but that is what I said. It is true that I was taken in, because I was coming back from Hvar. I was looking for my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you HVO then or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think there needs to be some clarification as to time here. Mr. Krsnik is talking about this witness being taken to Ljubuski on the 20th of May. I don't think there's anything in the record that suggests he was taken to the -- taken to Ljubuski on the 20th of May, 1993. Mr. Krsnik may be referring to another --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies to interpretation. I believe perhaps Mr. Krsnik is referring to another time when this witness was arrested by the Croats on May 20, 1992, almost a year earlier. So if there's going to be questions about this, I think counsel should be clear about the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, would you please clear it up for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. My learned friend is always a step in front of me. My next question precisely was to clear up the question whether it was 1992 or 1993. So with my next question, we'll clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So I'm talking about page 8. My learned friend managed to confuse me. My question was clear. In 1993 -- it is page 8, fifth paragraph. As of the 20th of the May, 1992, you ended up in the same building, the KP Dom. That's what you said. "We ended up at the KP Dom, Ljubuski, the centre for juvenile delinquents, where I had already been in May 1992."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I call it, the KP Dom. I am not sure that that is what it is. That's what I said. I can't exactly remember which building it was in Ljubuski or even if it was in Mostar. I said that I was taken to the same building I was taken to in May 1992. I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you specifically said that on both occasions it was the penal correctional centre, and this time you even further elaborated, saying that it was a centre for juvenile delinquents, and you also added, "Where I had already been in 1992. It was the old penitentiary."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the gentleman asked me what I meant by "KP Dom," and I explained what it was, a centre for juvenile delinquents or something like that, whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It's what you called it, not me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there was something like that also in Stolac. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In Ljubuski there is a penitentiary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in Stolac as well. I know very well the building I was in in 1992 and 1993. It's something I will not forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Be kind enough and tell us, in 1992, which uniform were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The uniform of the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So let's go back to page 3. You said very clearly and explicitly, I was wearing a uniform of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after that, the Patriotic League developed into the army, and it has an insignia on one side. And on the other side, there was the Defence Forces of the municipality. Something I'm not ashamed of. You can show a picture of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When did you abandon HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Prozor was attacked in 1992, in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you were simultaneously in the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until General Kraljevic was killed, I thought we were one and the same army. We were jointly defending ourselves against the same enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And which army were you in from September '93 until May -- no, sorry, not September. September '92, was it, until May '93?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was a freelance. I was nowhere. I didn't want to take part in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you were not a member of any army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until roughly the beginning of April '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And then you joined what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because in this statement -- and you also testified in court similarly; now we hear for the first time you joined the BH army in April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see you are interested in that. These gentlemen on this side did not inquire about that, and now I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Surely I'm under oath here. I have to tell you the truth. I don't know your name, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, did you have an apartment in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an apartment in a part of Mostar. It's not a proper apartment; a small studio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Where was that, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The part of town, Mr. President. I'm referring to, Your Honours, in very general terms, whether it was the West Bank or the East Bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that, but the reply from this witness might disclose his identity. If you need it, we can go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, just for this question, please, yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor, when he was examining this witness about the apartment he lived in, we were not in private session. The witness told us where he was, in which apartment, on the 10th of May. But anyway, I will abide by your ruling. It's better for us to go into private session than to make any errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: May I ask you who gave you that apartment? Did you get it as a refugee or as a soldier or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The apartment? I paid the rent out of my salary, sir. It cost about 100, 120 marks always.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you. I understand. Tell me, please, we are now in April 1993. You said that you went to the western part of Mostar on a daily basis, until the 10th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not absolutely every day, but we did -- I did go across, like everyone else, after the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When did the attack occur against the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in the morning, early in the morning on the 9th of May, 1993, without looking it up in the statement. I don't need to look it up. I know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me. But on page 4, you said explicitly that the building was attacked on the 18th of April in the evening. That's why I'm asking you that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Page 4, last paragraph. Please read, read what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first attack on the Vranica building, that's what I said. And to the Prosecutor, he said what happened between the 18th and the 23rd. That's my first statement. You asked me the exact real attack on the Vranica building. There were several attacks, you see. I personally was interested in the attack that took place on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But in your statement, you mentioned the 9th as an all-out attack on Mostar. You don't mention the Vranica building at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The all-out attack by the Croatian army against the town of Mostar. Surely Vranica was also in the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough and tell us how you know that Mr. Ejup Ganic, on the 18th of April, actually signed an agreement of some kind in the town of Mostar? And you testified about that in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, after the first truce, Mr. Ganic came to Mostar, and that a joint HVO and the BH army command was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my private affair. Do I have to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I see. That's your private affair. Very well. Thank you. You mentioned in your examination-in-chief a certain person called Splico, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you said that you also met him as a prisoner at the Heliodrom. Is it then that you learned that he was born in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was born in Mostar, that he's fair, that his front teeth were missing, that he was shorter than 1 metre 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you this question because, in your examination-in-chief, you said that he was a Splico, and he spoke with a Dalmatian accent.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did speak with a Dalmatian accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So when you were in the prison in Heliodrom, you didn't manage to learn where he was from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he wasn't in the same room as I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But he was in the same camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the central prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you didn't manage to find out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't interest me. All I know was that he was called Splico, and he spoke with a Dalmatian accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell me - I shall try and shorten this cross-examination - who guarded the Heliodrom, who were your guards and the people you communicated with? What unit did they belong to? Let me Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not go back into all the details, Marjanovic and all the others.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what unit? The military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. And the people that you mentioned from the warden, deputy warden, and so on, they also belonged to the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of one civilian, I think he was the Warden Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And all the others were military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, a final question for you: When did you tell the Prosecutor -- the gentleman who examined you in-chief, when did you tell the whole truth, on Friday when you discussed the statement you gave to the investigators? Was it on Friday, or Thursday, or when you arrived in The Hague? When did you tell him the whole truth about your stay at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to when you say "the truth."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When did you tell the Prosecutor the whole truth about the time you spent at the Heliodrom; when you came here in The Hague, on Thursday or Friday? I don't know when you arrived here, nor am I interested in that, actually. I'm just asking you. Let me rephrase it. You told the Prosecutor the whole truth when you came here and discussed your testimony here? It was only then that you told him that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Zelimir Par, and I am a lawyer and one of the counsel for the accused Vinko Martinovic. I would like to ask you some questions concerning your testimony. And I would like to begin with the incident at the Mostar police station when you said that you were abused by a group of soldiers, including persons called Romeo Blazevic and Ernest Takac. My question is, could you please tell us once again who else did you recognise on that occasion, apart from those two, their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Beno, and another's name was Jadranko. Somebody said he was Lovric, and later on I found out his full name was Jadranko Lovric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, could you, perhaps, identify the number one, who issued orders of those persons, who was the leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean of those names that I gave you? Mr. Beno took me in person to make a statement. Mr. Beno brought me to the room where a certain videotape was shown. What they had to do with him, I don't know. It is difficult for me to speak about that because horrible things happened to me then so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. I am not trying to remind you of that incident. I'm asking you about the relationship among them, about who was number one. And if I understand well, it was Beno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, if you're talking about Beno, it was Takac and Romeo Blazevic - their names I learned later on from some other people - to me were chieftains. But it all reminds me of what I went through, sir, and I cannot but remember all that now that you mention all these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: All right, all right. Can you tell us who was in charge of the prisoners in the Mostar police? Was it a civilian police, was it a military police, was it the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I know who brought me from my relatives' flat to the police station, and I assume, if it is the police building, then it must have been somebody in the police who was in charge. But I also know that it was the Croatian army people who came to this police building, and they were there in the immediate vicinity, 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You were brought there by the members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian army, but then I was taken over by Vinko Beno, who is a member of the police, and the building was the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Right. Did you see what kind of uniforms Blazevic and Takac wore on that occasion? Did you see any patches on them or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, because I saw them first when I entered, they were standing to the side. They were also wearing camouflage uniforms like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But did they have perhaps any patch indicating their unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I cannot remember really if there was anything to tell which unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: These two, Blazevic and Takac, you saw them again at Ljubuski, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, please, when you saw them at Ljubuski, do you remember if they came as part of a unit or did the two of them come on their own? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I'd be Alfred Hitchcock, the greatest director of all times, if I knew which unit they'd come with. I know they came in plain daylight. I know they were standing in a compound in the prison, and they beat some and took away others, and it was then that I found out once and for all that those gentlemen were who they were, that is, Romeo Blazevic and Takac. And it was said by their good friend who told me that. He said that they were his good friends, the man who stood next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So, please, I'm asking you. I wanted to find out whether they'd come on their own or under a commander, whether they'd come with a group. Not a unit and its name, but simply want to know whether they just turned up or did they come in a group? Did they seem to have a leader, a commander, or was it just the two of them who turned up there in plain daylight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. We are standing in a compound -- I have to explain it to you. It's a camp. It's camp, not a normal situation. And if you're standing in a circle -- we all stand in a circle, and you're allowed only to look down, how can I know who they came with and how? All I know is they came very close to me and they'd asked a gentleman who was standing next to me certain things, and all I know is that those persons -- the faces of those persons, and I'll never forget them, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about it, that you'll never forget their faces, could you please describe them to us in a few words, first Romeo and then Ernest.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Romeo is a gentleman who was more on the fair side, light brown, slightly shorter than Ernest Takac. Ernest Takac is very strongly built. His hair was black. When I saw him, he had a few days' stubble. The first time I saw him, he didn't have any beard or anything. Ernest Takac is a very powerfully-built man.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And in Ljubuski, who guarded prisoners? Was it the police or the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were policemen of some kind, military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Could you explain it to us? Do you know how is it that the two of them, Romeo and Ernest, could pass by those policemen and come into direct contact with prisoners? How is it they were allowed to do that? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't a military policeman to know such things. I'm just a humble mortal who is kept in a prison and is kept locked up and goes out only when he needs to get out. I cannot come out as I please. It's only when somebody comes and says, "You're allowed to come out," then I do come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, I'm fully aware of that situation. It is perfectly legitimate for you to tell us that you don't know when you don't know something. But, all right, tell us. Let's try, to try to clear it up for the Chamber and all that. How far is the town of Ljubuski from the town of Mostar? How far are they, two towns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell the truth, I think it's about -- it's some 40 kilometres or so south-west of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like us to go back to the Heliodrom, to your part -- to your testimony about the Heliodrom. When you said sometime in mid-June 1993, during your stay at the Heliodrom, and that you saw that day Vinko Martinovic, Stela, in front of Heliodrom, now, my question is: Did I understand you well when you said that you saw him in front of Heliodrom, that is, not within the compound but in front of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. As far as I can remember, I did not say that I saw him at the entrance into the -- the western entrance into the central prison, not in front of the Heliodrom, because I'd need binoculars to see him from the room that I was in to see Mr. Stela there. I know I saw him in front of the building. Perhaps there is a slight mistake in the interpretation. I know that the gentleman came from the western side of it, from the so-called basketball ground, to the central prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And will you tell us what he looked like then? What kind of uniform did he wear? Was he armed? Could you describe him a little?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was wearing what everybody else was wearing. So a camouflage uniform like everybody else. And he came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: From my notes, you -- according to my notes, you said that you saw him when prisoners were being brought in a truck or something.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in; taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see. Taken out. But who then -- who brought those prisoners to the truck? Was it the policemen who escorted them or the soldiers? Who escorted those prisoners to the truck and turned them over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, those men, those men who were in the central prison. Those who enter a room and say, "Let's go," ten, 20, 30 men who have to go to work, because it's not voluntary. So the policeman says, "You, you, and you." So what can I do? And I go out to work. Nobody asks me what I want to do. So it is the gentlemen, policemen, messers. policemen who were in the central prison. They took them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes. That was my question, whether it was a policeman, whether those people who took you to the trucks were policemen, and you say yes, that is, military policemen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Please, don't misunderstand me. I think you are trying to play games with me. I know well what I said, that it was Mr. Stela who came in mid-July to the Heliodrom, because he needed some workers to go to a certain area to work. And then you asked me left and right, whether it was these or those. I know that a policeman enters a room and says, "You, you, you, and you are going to work," and I know that it was the military policeman who was doing a shift at that moment in the prison who took me out, and one knows who were the military policemen in the prison at the time. There were some at some -- Ante Buhovac or Puce, some Smiljanic or Slavko Skender, Marjanovic. There were not five of them, but I'm just mentioning those that I know. So they came, and it was the policemen, policemen who escorted me from the building to the truck. I saw Mr. Stela, who was standing on the right side of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to make a pause, I mean in the questions and answers, because you give a difficult time to the interpreters, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours. I'll bear it in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Witness, that was precisely my question, that is, I'm not playing any games with you. I'm not trying to frame you or anything. I'm asking you whether Vinko Martinovic, Stela, entered the cells in the prison, took prisoners from there and took them to the truck, or did Vinko Martinovic wait by the truck and military policemen escorted the prisoners to the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd be the biggest liar in the world if I said that Mr. Stela had come to a certain room and taken me out of it. Mr. Stela wasn't the one who took me out of the room. It was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Right. Let's move on. You, therefore, board the truck, and you arrive at Jadranko Lovric's coffee bar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediate vicinity. Excuse me. Immediate vicinity of Jadranko Lovric's coffee bar. Not into the coffee bar of Jadranko Lovric, immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: On that occasion, in the immediate vicinity of Jadranko Lovric's coffee bar, was Mr. Salko Osmic in the same group with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, please, do you know what happened to Salko Osmic later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salko Osmic left with a group - I wasn't in it - and I think he was one of the few who survived from that group. Mustafa Cilic, called Cile, Rasim Lulic. I'm talking about people, of course, that I know, sir, and who I think are on the list of the missing as far as I know. But Salko Osmic, I saw him return after a long time, to the Heliodrom just prior to my escape from the Heliodrom. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, this Salko Osmic, testifying in public before this Court on the 26th and 7th of September, he testified about his detention, his labour duty, and so on and so forth, but in his testimony, he never ever mentioned seeing Stela, Stela - excuse me - or, rather, that incident. So my question to you is: Are you positive that Salko Osmic was with you on that particular occasion? And if so, would he have any reason to keep silent about it, not to tell this Court about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what Salko was asked about it. I did not see Salko since 1994, when he came out of camp. So I don't know. I only speak about what I saw. And I knew Mr. Stela personally, because he was born in the municipality of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But you say that he was in that group of prisoners who were taken and some of whom went missing. And so I wish to ask you: Do you know where these people were taken, that other group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group, roughly -- I'm not sure whether it was seven or nine or ten men who left with Mr. Stela. I know they were taken somewhere, but I was taken to Dzubrani at that time to work there, so I had no idea where those people were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Right. Did you perhaps hear that they were taken to the village of Vojno, that they -- that somebody saw them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from some people, from that self-same Salko Osmic when he returned. I think he said that he'd been to the village of Vojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. And tell me, do you know which army unit was quartered in Vojno?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know -- have you heard of the 2nd HVO battalion? Would you say that it was possible that they were in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not know which unit it was. In that area, as far as I could remember, the name that I know, I mean one of the commanders, I believe he commanded the company. And that name is Zlatko Gavro -- Zdenko Gavro, excuse me. But which unit he was, I really don't know. Which battalion, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know which positions were manned by Stela's unit? I believe it was mentioned they were somewhere near the Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Slezak, the Mrmak unit. I know what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But my question is how far is it from the Health Centre to the village of Vojno? Do you know the distance between those two places, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from the centre of the town to the village of Vojno? It is on the west side of Mostar. Well, it can't be less than seven kilometres. Could be more. Northwest of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I see. Let's go back to the fate of those -- to the lot of those people. Did you ever personally try to check what happened to those people, which ones of them survived and who are still missing, or is it just some stories that went around that you heard and that you never tried to verify them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I lived in Jablanica for a while. I worked there in October 1993. And when some of those men arrived from the camp, then naturally I saw those people. I socialised with them, those men from Sovici whom I met in the camp, and some I had known before. So naturally, I wanted to know, as a human being, about who had come out of the camp and who hadn't come out of the camp. As far as I can remember, a chap called Mustafa Cilic, Cile everybody called him. I'm not sure whether he's Mustafa or Mujo or Mohamed or something. But I know that he was Cile. He was very young. He had curly hair, and that he disappeared, that he was in the camp with me, that he left with those ten men taken away by Mr. Stela, and they simply disappeared. How they went missing, who is the responsibility, I really don't know, and I didn't ask. I didn't try to inquire about that because I was afraid it might try to hurt his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Precisely. As you keep pointing out, Mr. Stela took them away, Mr. Stela this, Mr. Stela that, and those people went missing. Now, my client Stela asked me to clear it up with you. You've come here -- have you come here to accuse him of being responsible for the fate of those people? Because you say Stela took him away, so I hold him responsible for that death. Or is it something else? And I need to clear it up with you here. So my question is quite plain to you: When you speak about the lot of these people, are you claiming that Vinko Martinovic is responsible for them, that he was with them throughout? Or would you allow that the fate of these people perhaps depended on some other -- was determined by some other circumstances, by some other events, developments, in our units and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, you have to understand that this witness is going to give us the facts, rather than conclusions. It is the Trial Chamber that will make the conclusions. We don't want you to ask any questions concerning any speculations or the conclusions from this witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I withdraw the question, then. Now, I'd like to ask to go briefly into private session, please, because I want to show the witness a document and ask about two or three things that are in this document. His name is on the document, so I would like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have it here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it is time, so we'll adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott. Re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness HH, just a very few questions. Just to clarify for the record the date of some cease-fire or peace agreement, if we can call it that, that was signed by Ejup Ganic, just so the record is clear, was that, to your recollection, signed, as far as you know, on the 23rd of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I have about two or three other questions that I think we'll have to go into private session on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could I ask you, either Mr. Scott or Mr. Par -- can I ask Mr. Scott or Mr. Par about the document which has been described as Defence document D2/14? Did that document have a date on its original version?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If Mr. Par can assist, he can also certainly do so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. I cannot find a date on the document. There is a reference -- well, there might be a date. Again maybe Mr. Par can -- there may be a stamp on the document dated the 19th of December, 1993, but I'm not -- I'm not sure about that, and I'm not prepared to say that that's necessarily the case, but it could -- it appears that it might be that. It appears there's also a date, Judge Clark, Your Honour, on the first paragraph. There's a reference to the 8th of November, 1993. So I suppose one would have to draw the conclusion or could draw the conclusion that the document would have had to have been prepared at least after the 8th of November, but I'm sorry, I don't think I can assist further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, there's another date on the 12th of November, '93, but I wondered, seeing that that document was furnished to the Defence by the Prosecution, if somebody has the original and if any date appears on that. But I think you said you think there's a stamp that could read the 19th of December, '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think so. What I will do, Your Honour, I think I've exhausted what I can do to assist the Chamber, but I can make further inquiries if there's a better document -- better copy available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, do you agree that the stamp might read the 19th of the 12th, '93?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that is the only relevant date. There's a stamp saying that this document was received on the 19th of December, '93, and it has a number for the Defence Department of the Security and Information Service, and I also see a stamp of the archives along the lines the Prosecutor has said. So I consider this date to be the relevant one, the 19th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Par. That's good enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no problem, if it will assist the Chamber. I can tender a copy of the B/C/S version where you can see what Mr. Par and I are both referring to. The usher just left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm greatly assisted by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, as you notice, Mr. Par gave the only two English copies which were provided by the Prosecutor to Madam Registrar, so would it be possible later to have a copy in English for each one of us? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you have a copy of the Bosnian version of that in front of you, that document? You do. Did you have a chance to look at it during the break, or did it remain on the desk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could you give it a quick glance now and look at the names of persons who were alleged to have escaped. There's a list of six originally, and then it's followed by a list of the soldier accompanying the escapee. So could you look at that list of names.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the usher to switch on the other microphone of the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, if you've had a chance to have a look at that, I notice that there are more than 30 names of people who are alleged to have escaped. And obviously, included in that list is your own name, and I recognise another witness's name, or I think I do. Can you say, looking at that list, whether from your own knowledge that you know that people did escape who are on that list, or from your own knowledge, that they, in fact, died or were injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, before me, Ahmet Penava had escaped. After me, as far as I know, Mustafa Begic escaped, Asim Jazvin, and Semir Toljaga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So from your knowledge, one name you recognise as being a legitimate escapee, and three perhaps after you. If you look at that list again, are there any on that list who are described as having escaped who you know to have been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Asim Jasvin was killed. I think that Dzemal Taso died. I know that he died of natural causes, but whether he escaped -- I don't know that he escaped from the Heliodrom. I don't know that. And he is listed here -- I know that Mr. Penava escaped. And Dzemal Taso, I'm not so sure -- I don't know whether he escaped, but I know that the gentleman died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we'll leave that list aside. You told us on Thursday of -- and you were unwilling to talk about it, of your ill-treatment and torture in the stone building and then at the Heliodrom at Ljubuski, and I think you told us at one stage that you'd been there for a while when you were registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. You mentioned the Ljubuski building as being the place where I was beaten and registered, but I was registered at the Heliodrom and not at Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were registered at the Heliodrom, could you assist the Trial Chamber in telling us how that came about and whether you had an opportunity to speak to representatives from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a room that we were in and that they entered, there were representatives of the Red Cross, but at the same time, there were representatives present of the police. So we really didn't dare talk much, as far as I can remember, to the gentlemen from the Red Cross. I think that some people even wrote some messages to the Red Cross for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I can understand if the policemen were present while the representatives from the Red Cross were there it would be difficult for you to discuss anything, but did the representative from the Red Cross see or notice your injuries? This is not yours personally, but in the group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the name of the person. I keep trying to remember the name of the person who spoke English or some other language, probably English or French, and who spoke to a person, a person from the Red Cross. And afterwards, I know that that person came up to me and he sort of interpreted partly, and I went out to the sort of corridor in the building. I lifted up my T-shirt and my trousers to above my knees. That's as much as I managed to show of my injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So you did show your injuries to somebody.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a short woman of some 55, roughly. That is my estimate. But this was after talking to this person whose name I'm trying to remember. She was, I think, also from Central Bosnia. I just cannot remember her name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about her name, but what I really wanted to know is did the Red Cross people have an opportunity to discover that many of you had injuries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were not allowed to. I was among the few who had the courage and went up there to show it to them. That's as much as I was able to see. I don't think I was allowed. We just filled in these cards of the Red Cross, and I managed to sneak out into the corridor and, as I said, to lift up my trousers and my T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. Did the representative from the Red Cross say anything to you or to the guards in your presence about the treatment of prisoners of war and the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were people there who were infiltrated amongst us. We didn't dare. We didn't dare say anything, as far as I can remember. All I can remember is when they came and what I did in the corridor. After this talk of this young man who was maybe my age or maybe a little younger, he was also tall, and he spoke with this lady, and after this conversation, he said to me -- he made a sign, and I showed my injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did this woman from the Red Cross say to any of you that your position was protected by international convention or treaty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would say that to us, that we were protected, and once we were registered that we would be protected. Unfortunately, after the registration and continued torture at the Heliodrom, more than a thousand and a half people went missing from Mostar, who were killed and went missing, and most of them had been registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was that the only visit that you had from the Red Cross? Did anybody come back to check that the same people who were on the list were still alive and present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, while I was there, it was the one and only time that I personally saw the Red Cross as regards me and this group I was in. Possibly they may have come later. I believe they did, because they brought some messages. After we had filled in these cards and after we were registered, I'm not sure when, but maybe seven or 15 days later, individuals amongst us did receive messages, answers to the messages they had written, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, if I can bring you a little bit beyond that to when you were describing how the police would come into your cell and select people for forced labour, and just, as you've described, point out, "You, you, and you," and they would take approximately 30 people. Now, I want you to think about this: When the policemen did this, did any of them record the names of the prisoners or the internees who were taken out for work duty and sign for them? Was there a procedure, a formal procedure for taking out the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I'm telling you what I know and what I remember. I think only when we went to work south of the town of Mostar where the bridge was being built that I worked on, too. The bridge on the Neretva River itself where the Buna River flows into the Neretva River, and I think that only in that case it was known exactly the number of people who were going and it always had to be the same people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And on that occasion when you saw a record being kept of the people who went, was there a record also kept of the people who returned, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in this particular case. I know that Mr. -- Mr. -- I can't remember the name now, the gentleman who was responsible for that area. His name was Rafo. He had a brother living in Buna. I'm sorry for elaborating. I know his father was massacred by the Serbs in 1992. Gagro. His brother's name was Srecko Gagro, and the other one is Rafo Gagro. So I know he was in charge of that building site in the location called Buna, where the Buna River flows into the Neretva River, and where I worked for at least seven days doing heavy labour in water with very little food. And it was only in that case that there was a record of who was going, and other people could not go because they needed people who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. familiar with building work, who could use a compressor. We were drilling holes. And I think it was Mr. Rafo who was in charge -- no, I don't think so; I'm a hundred percent sure he supervised things. He did the mining work. We did the other heavy duty. That was that one case that it was known who was going, and that was for the Buna River. And he would walk in early in the morning and say, "Let's go to Buna."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask you directly arising out of your response, and in relation to the Buna River, was this a situation where any of the prisoners were liable to be shot at by either the Serbs or the ABiH? Were you in danger of being caught in direct fire or crossfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at Buna itself, we were not in immediate danger. Actually, I have to elaborate. At Buna actually, I don't think -- at least, when I went there, until more or less the very beginning of July, I don't think that there was any real immediate danger for people's lives there, only if the Serb side would fire a shell or so. But I think they got on so well in destroying Bosnia-Herzegovina that they didn't need to shell the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So can I -- I take it from that that the only occasion in the period that you were a prisoner that you can recall a record being made of prisoners taken to carry out labour was the occasion when there was no danger of being caught in crossfire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, at Buna. That is true. The only place where I was recorded, where my name was recorded, when somebody checked when I returned, was the location of Buna and the bridge on the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: During the period that you were a prisoner in either of the camps and that you were taken out to perform labour, did you ever perform tasks which could be described as non-dangerous and municipal tasks, like tidying up a playground or cleaning the streets or planting shrubs; municipal work? Can any of the forced labour that you did be described as those sort of civilian works?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You are absolutely positive about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'm a hundred percent sure, except for this case. I'm a hundred percent sure that I didn't go anywhere voluntarily to work, and I'm a hundred percent sure that I never went anywhere to do cleaning work or planting or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I'm asking you those questions because of evidence that we've received from other sources, so I was just checking that with you. That doesn't mean that I'm not believing what you say. I don't want you to think that. It's just that we've seen some documents which would appear to indicate otherwise. But thank you very much, indeed, for your assistance. And I wish you well in your new life, wherever it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. A part of my questions have already been put; however, I would like to ask the witness, after having said that the work he did at the Buna River was hard work but not dangerous, their lives were not at risk, could he tell me whether those works had to do with the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the bridge -- I mean, explosives were handled there; and people who handled explosives, they knew what that was. And I, who worked with the drilling machine, I knew how to use that. I knew how to drill holes for explosives. Others were putting up boarding for the concrete pillars for the bridge. So of course, it was possible to be hit by stray shots -- shell. But I repeat, at the time when the Croatian state committed aggression against the Bosnian state, I don't think that a single Serbian shell hit the Croatian side. I don't think there was any such case, and they went along so perfectly destroying Bosnian homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my second question: In that fixed cemetery where people were buried without distinction as to religion or ethnicity, where you were at that cemetery where the HVO soldiers and the prisoners, when they were mingled? That is, when you were put amongst the soldiers of the HV, could you then tell me, on that occasion, who were -- what were the accused and their companions doing at that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were coming in our direction from the opposite side. They were walking towards that group. And I was the second behind the gentlemen. That is, there were two soldiers, two Croatian soldiers, then two of us and so on and so forth. We alternated, a civilian, a Croat soldier, and then another civilian. We were all mingled. That was the first time that that happened at that place. It was in a sort of a zigzag line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that. I understand this mingling of the detainees and the HVO. I'm asking about Mr. Naletilic and others doing that. Did you say that you were just moving and you merely met in that place? I'm asking, what were they doing? Were they engaged in any activity there? Did you simply meet, they coming from the north, you from the south, and your paths simply crossed over, or were they doing something? Were they engaged in any kind of activity? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that we met there. Whether they were engaged in any kind of activity, I really do not know. I know it was ours to move towards the Kantarevac stadium to do certain things there, that we had shovels with us, pickaxes and things. And that is in the immediate vicinity of the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Diarra. Any questions out of the Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. Not for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I do not have any questions, Your Honours. I merely wanted to ask, with the leave of the Honourable Court, we looked at the transcript and we -- the names of people I asked in my question. So I'd like to go into private session to have those names established. If not, then I can resolve it in some other way, just to check the names that I mentioned. They are not in the transcript. I do not have any questions, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I will give you the opportunity to check all those names, but it's only limited to those names. We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for helping us by giving your evidence. We all wish you good luck in the future. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will take you out of the room. Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender from both sides? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only document that was marked by the Prosecution with this witness was a marked version of Exhibit 12, which he made a number "1" and number "2" on, and consistent with past practice - excuse me - I would ask the registrar to give that an appropriate subnumber so that it is Exhibit 12 point something, whatever that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So that would be 12/1/1 and 12/2/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure why there would be two but -- there's only one exhibit, but whatever numbers appropriate would be. There's an Exhibit 12 and then there should be a marked version, a marked Exhibit 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe after the session you can consult with Madam Registrar regarding those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand well, it is the map that was drawn by the witness. No, no objections. But I should, at the same time, like to tender as a Defence exhibit the statement of the 1st of May, 1994, number 1/31, to tender it as a Defence exhibit. It is the statement given on the 1st of April, '94. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, as you know, there's a decision pending on the previous statement made by the witness. So before that, we could give it an ID number, but we cannot admit it into the evidence at this stage. I hope you could understand. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not object, and we should also like to tender Document D2/14, the list that we discussed of persons who escaped from detention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that this document should be put under seal. Any objections from Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We would agree that it be under seal. The Prosecution has no objection to D2/14. As, Mr. President, you've already anticipated, we continue to have the same standing objection as to the prior statements. In this particular case, I would simply add that, in addition to our usual objections, we would also object further that this is a statement which there has been -- there is no evidence in the record connecting that statement to this witness at all. But we have our usual objection. And I wonder, Mr. President, if I could -- there's something I might be able to assist the Chamber with, but I would have to go into private session just for a moment before the next witness comes in, if you would agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So that D2/14 is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me the floor. The statement that I tendered, and about which my learned friend says has nothing to do with the witness, I wish to say that that is not true. It has to do with the witness and how, and that is why the Defence tendered it. Of course, it has to do with this witness, and I believe in a very important way, too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your views. Could we go to the private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 12.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you hear me? Can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. I have a piece of paper which contains your name and also the pseudonym which you have been given, because the Trial Chamber has granted the request for you to testify under protective measures. So at this time, I'm going to ask you to look at the paper and, without saying your name, simply tell us whether your name correctly appears on that paper with your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Witness, your pseudonym is, I believe, II, and so for our purposes in these proceedings, we'll be referring to you with that pseudonym, and you should not say your name or the names of your family members during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, as that paper is circulated, Mr. President, with your permission, I could give a brief resume or summary to the Trial Chamber in terms of the relevant parts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The testimony of Witness II will be relevant to paragraphs 7 and 11 of the indictment, which are a part of the Background of the indictment relating to international armed conflict and the campaign, widespread and systematic. Also, Superior Authority of the accused under paragraphs 16 and 17. Paragraphs 18 through 21 of the General Allegations, which relate to international armed conflict and the existence of a widespread or systematic campaign. The testimony is relevant to paragraphs 27 and 28 of count 1, which relate to the various detention facilities that were established throughout the Western Herzegovina region. Also in count 1, the testimony is relevant to paragraphs 30 and 34, paragraph 30 being the headquarters of the accused Martinovic in the city of Mostar. The testimony will also be relevant to paragraphs 35 to 38 of the indictment, which form part of counts 2 through 8 relating to the use of prisoners to perform labour and other tasks. Also, within counts 2 through 8, the testimony relates to paragraph 40 and 41. And then finally, the witness's testimony will relate to paragraph 57, which is count 21, charging looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed with your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, let me first ask you a couple of background questions about yourself. In 1993 -- 1992 -- excuse me. In 1993, were you a Bosnian Muslim who was a member of the HVO in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at that time, say, during May - in fact, April, May, June of 1993 - what was your rank and what was your -- what were your duties as a member of the HVO in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a soldier in the military police at the beginning for the first two or three months, and then I left the military police and was a soldier in the 1st battalion of the 4th Company, of the Knez Domagoj Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Directing your attention to the 1st of July, 1993, can you tell us, please, where you were deployed and what were your duties on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent the night on the front line, the separation line. And when I finished my shift in the morning, after the shift, I went to the medical centre with a colleague of mine. And on the way there, I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Who were you captured by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: By members also of the Knez Domagoj Brigade but a different company, the members of the 2nd Company of the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were other members of your unit also arrested on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were about 120 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And is there any particular reason why those individuals were arrested, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no problems, and we realised the reason later. All Muslims, almost all Muslims were arrested --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who didn't manage to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did -- and the persons arresting the Muslims -- let me first clarify or try to ask you to clarify. Are we talking about other Muslim members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of my unit and civilians also who were found there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And who were you and the others arrested by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said; members of the same brigade who took over from us on the front line when we finished our shift. They would come to replace us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: After you were arrested, then, were you taken to a different location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in front of the medical centre until they rounded us all up, and later we were driven to the camp at Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many Muslim members of your unit or Muslim civilians were arrested with you and taken to Dretelj on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the unit, the whole unit, 120 men, and about 20 to 30 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, then what occurred then after you and the others arrived at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We handed over all our personal documents, everything we had on us, everything we owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you wearing your HVO uniform when you arrived at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And were you -- did you continue then to wear that uniform after you were received at Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those of us who came in uniforms took off our uniforms and were given uniforms of the former JNA army which used to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What's the colour of those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Olive green. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's the colour of the uniforms of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, from this point forward, Witness, the 1st of July, let me ask you if you could tell us first, how long did you remain there at the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 21st of July, for 21 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during that period of time, where did you stay? Where were you held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a metal hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did other prisoners arrive at the camp on the 1st of July or in the days that followed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some on the 1st of July, all that day, and maybe for a week after that people were coming in on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you remained or were held in a metal hangar. Do you know approximately how many other prisoners were with you in that hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, 120 or 150 of us. Then there came a group from -- people who had already been arrested before that, 250. Then in the course of that day and the next day, we totalled about 450 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: At this time, I'd like to ask that the -- excuse me. At this time, I'd like to ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 21.8, which is a photograph. We can place this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, now, if the pointer is there with you on the desk, I wonder if you could use the pointer to show us the place where you were held, if you see it on this photograph. If you don't have the pointer, perhaps you could just use a pencil.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. Now I'm going to ask you to take the photograph, and using one of the markers that's next to the screen there, if you would place a circle around that hangar which you've just pointed to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in the few remaining minutes that we have left before the lunch break, I want to ask you to describe for us in general terms the conditions that existed during those 21 days that you were at the Dretelj camp in terms of food, personal sanitation, the general sorts of conditions that you had during those 21 days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hygienic conditions were very bad. We had nothing. We were able to wash once out of a truck tank which was standing here. We obtained a toilet seven or ten days later, and it was situated here. And the food and the water were a great problem. We were given one meal a day. A loaf of bread would be shared by about 15 to 16 people. The food came very hot, so you couldn't really eat it properly. We were given water after lunch, and one more time during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How much space did you and the other people have who were in this hangar for resting or sleeping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were lined up one against the other. We were -- it was possible to lie down, but there was very little space between us. But as there were so many of us, and it was a steel hangar, and there were many of us, the temperature was very high. And this had an adverse effect on us, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because of the high temperature and the heat, did you and the others have enough water to drink?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can continue or we can take a break at this time, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 2.30 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just before the break, you had begun to tell us about the situation that you found after your arrival with the others at the Dretelj camp. You were talking about food and water and the heat. I wanted to ask you whether the situation in the camp changed on or about the 13th of July, approximately two weeks after you arrived in the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how things changed and why they changed, if you know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There'd been some fighting about 10 kilometres outside Capljina. There was fighting between uncaptured Muslims who were trying to make a breakthrough to the Mostar territory on one side and HVO soldiers on the other, and both sides suffered losses. During those operations, we received no food or water for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during those three days, can you tell us how you and the others responded or were affected by the lack of food and water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were already very weak, and this merely exacerbated the situation in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: How did some of the prisoners react to that? How did they attempt to relieve their thirst?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They drank their own urine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'd like to ask you if during those 21 days at Dretelj you or others were beaten by the guards at the Dretelj camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, there were those cases, things what happened to other people, but once when some 20 of my -- of men from my unit tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And how did that affect you or the others who remained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when it was -- when their flight was discovered, that group -- a man came. He introduced himself as Commander Anicic, and split the rest of my unit into groups of 13 and distributed them around other rooms in the camp and started the interrogation of who had escaped, when did he escape, how did they escape, and with all that, some blows were dealt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you receive any blows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, during those three weeks in Dretelj, did you observe or hear of beatings taking place of other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was that a frequent occurrence or was it something that did not occur very often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the situation outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you -- perhaps you could explain that a little bit. What's the "situation"? How would that affect the beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when there was fighting on the ground, it would affect things in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again, if you could just -- just so we're clear exactly what you're saying, could you describe how events outside the camp could affect events inside the camp in respect of beatings, which is the topic I'm asking you about now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the 13th, that is, the losses suffered by both sides, drunk -- soldiers would arrive drunk and then harass and beat inmates, force them to drink alcohol as if it were water, took out some men, asked them if anyone -- any one of them was related to another captured person. So that the situation outside found its reflection in the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if prisoners were forced to beat other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what you know about that, what you saw, what you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw when two brothers were slapping one another, and I heard about a few other cases, but I did not eye witness them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know about another incident in which a prisoner named Repak was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is another thing that I heard about. He was engaged in a fight with another prisoner. But that again, I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: During the time that you were at Dretelj, did any shooting take place, that is, with firearms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fire, I guess, to intimidate, but it would be about a metre or a metre and a half above our heads, because we had been ordered to either sit or lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- first of all, you say you were sitting or lying down. Where were you at the time you were sitting and -- or lying down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the metal hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Approximately how many hours a day did you and the others stay inside that hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would come out before lunch, and then for the second time to drink some water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so those were the only two times during the day in which you were allowed outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you and the others -- that the shooting was taking place as you were sitting or laying down, where was the shooting coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS HH [Resumed]
utterances.text: From outside, from in front of the hangar.
